Compulsory, state-regulated schooling for all children—and a complete legal ban on homeschooling—is not an attack on families, religion, or individuality. It is a defense of children’s rights, educational quality, social cohesion, and protection from abuse and indoctrination. In a modern, complex democracy, education is too important to be left entirely to the private discretion of individual households. Just as we regulate food safety, medicine, and workplaces to protect vulnerable people, we must regulate education to safeguard children.

Below is a detailed case for why homeschooling should be legally banned and why every child should attend a state-regulated public or private school.

I. Education is a Right of the Child, Not the Property of the Parent

A foundational question in this debate is: whose interests come first—parents’ preferences or children’s rights?

Parents have an important, legitimate role in their children’s upbringing, but children are not property. They are independent persons with rights, including:

  • The right to a basic, high-quality education
  • The right to learn widely accepted scientific and historical knowledge
  • The right to acquire skills (literacy, numeracy, critical thinking) needed to be self-sufficient adults
  • The right to be exposed to a diversity of perspectives, not just those of their parents

The state has a duty to ensure that these rights are met, particularly because children cannot choose their parents, cannot easily leave home, and cannot advocate effectively for themselves. When parents educate at home without meaningful oversight, a child’s right to education becomes entirely contingent on the parents’ competence, goodwill, ideology, and emotional stability. That is too precarious.

Compulsory schooling in state-regulated institutions is not about distrusting all parents; it is about recognizing that:

  • Even loving parents can lack the knowledge or resources to provide a comprehensive education.
  • Some parents use homeschooling to conceal educational neglect, abuse, or extreme indoctrination.
  • Children deserve protections that do not depend on winning the “parent lottery.”

A legal ban on homeschooling shifts the legal presumption: society guarantees the child a minimum standard of education and safety, rather than hoping each family voluntarily provides it.

II. Standardized Education: Ensuring Quality and Protecting Against Neglect

Homeschooling allows education to vary wildly in quality—from excellent to catastrophically inadequate—with very little accountability. By contrast, state-regulated schools, whether public or private, provide at least a baseline of:

  • Qualified teachers trained in pedagogy and subject matter
  • Structured curricula aligned with educational standards
  • Regular assessments to ensure children are progressing
  • External oversight and correction when things go wrong

A. Academic Content and Competence

In homeschool settings, parents may:

  • Lack expertise in math, science, or languages beyond elementary levels
  • Fail to keep pace with changing knowledge and pedagogical methods
  • Cherry-pick or omit subjects based on personal beliefs (e.g., skipping evolution, civics, sex education, or critical thinking)

Even well-intentioned parents can underestimate the complexity of providing a comprehensive, balanced education, especially at the middle and high school levels. A teenager deserves teachers who actually understand algebra, biology, literature analysis, and world history at a competent level—not just whatever their parents remember from decades ago.

The reality is that in many jurisdictions, homeschool oversight is minimal or nonexistent. Parents can pull a child out of school with no requirement to:

  • Show qualifications
  • Follow an accredited curriculum
  • Submit to standardized testing
  • Allow external evaluation of learning outcomes

A legal ban on homeschooling, coupled with mandatory attendance in regulated schools, is the surest way to guarantee that all children receive at least a minimally adequate education, regardless of parental capacity or ideology.

III. Socialization and Civic Integration: Preparing Children for Life in a Diverse Democracy

Education is not just about individual academic achievement. It is also about preparing children to live among others: to understand different viewpoints, cooperate across differences, resolve conflicts nonviolently, and participate responsibly in civic life.

A. Social Skills and Emotional Development

Schools are structured social environments where children:

  • Interact with peers from different backgrounds
  • Learn to share resources, wait their turn, and collaborate in groups
  • Negotiate friendships, disagreements, and rules
  • Encounter adults other than their parents—teachers, counselors, administrators

These experiences build social skills and emotional resilience that are very hard to replicate in an isolated home environment.

Homeschooling often means:

  • Limited exposure to peers or interactions only with carefully selected families who share similar beliefs and backgrounds.
  • Socialization shaped almost entirely by parents’ preferences, limiting a child’s ability to encounter and navigate genuine difference.

This can leave homeschool children poorly prepared for university, workplaces, and broader society, where they will inevitably meet people who do not share their family’s views, culture, or religion.

B. Civic Education and Pluralism

Democratic societies require citizens who:

  • Understand basic civic principles and rights
  • Can evaluate information and resist misinformation
  • Recognize the legitimacy of people who live, believe, or vote differently
  • Feel some shared identity and responsibility with fellow citizens

State-regulated schools—especially public schools—are one of the few institutions where children from different ideological, ethnic, and socioeconomic backgrounds regularly meet and learn together under common rules.

Homeschooling, especially when motivated by religious or ideological separation from mainstream society, can:

  • Encourage echo chambers and insulation from broader perspectives
  • Reinforce us-versus-them worldviews
  • Undermine a sense of shared civic identity and responsibility

A legal requirement that all children attend regulated schools is an investment in social cohesion, civic literacy, and democratic stability.

IV. Protection Against Abuse, Neglect, and Extremist Indoctrination

One of the most compelling arguments for banning homeschooling is the protection of vulnerable children from abuse, neglect, and harmful indoctrination that can go completely unseen when education happens behind closed doors.

A. Schools as a Safeguard

Schools are not just educational institutions; they are also:

  • Places where mandated reporters (teachers, counselors, nurses) can notice signs of physical, sexual, or emotional abuse.
  • Environments where a child has daily contact with adults outside the family, providing opportunities to disclose mistreatment.
  • Settings where developmental problems, mental health issues, or learning disabilities can be identified and addressed.

When children are homeschooled, these safety nets weaken dramatically. Abusive or neglectful parents can:

  • Avoid scrutiny by claiming to homeschool, especially in places with minimal regulation.
  • Limit their children’s contact with any outside authority who might intervene.
  • Conceal truancy, domestic violence, or extreme ideological indoctrination under the guise of “parental rights.”

A ban on homeschooling ensures that every child is seen regularly by trained professionals who can recognize and respond to red flags.

B. Shielding Children from Extremism

While many homeschooling families are not extremists, some do use homeschooling to:

  • Isolate children from any information that contradicts a rigid ideological or religious narrative.
  • Teach historical revisionism, conspiracy theories, or intolerance as unquestionable truth.
  • Inculcate beliefs that openly reject the legitimacy of democratic institutions, other faiths, or entire groups of people.

The state cannot—and should not—control private belief. But it has a legitimate interest in ensuring that children are not denied exposure to basic scientific facts, historical realities, and the existence of legitimate disagreement in a pluralistic society.

Mandatory attendance in regulated schools, with standardized curricula and oversight, makes it much harder to raise children in closed informational environments where they lack the tools to eventually make informed choices for themselves.

V. Equity and Social Cohesion: Education as a Shared Social Project

Education is a public good, not just a private family matter. When significant numbers of families opt out of common institutions like public schools:

  • Social divides deepen; children grow up more segregated by class, ideology, and religion.
  • Public support for adequately funding and improving schools can weaken (those who leave feel less invested).
  • The idea that we owe each other’s children something—a fair chance, basic skills, and mutual understanding—erodes.

A universal requirement to attend regulated schools reinforces the principle that:

  • Society has a shared responsibility to educate all its young.
  • Children from different backgrounds deserve to learn together, not in separate silos.
  • The public system must be good enough for everyone’s children, which incentivizes continuous improvement.

Homeschooling, especially by more privileged families, can contribute to educational fragmentation and inequality: those with time, money, and education can craft customized environments for their own children, while others are left to struggle in underfunded systems. A ban, combined with robust investment in both public and regulated private schools, pushes us toward a more just and cohesive educational landscape.

VI. Addressing Common Counterarguments

1. “Parents know what’s best for their children.”

Parents often know their children’s personalities and needs better than anyone. But “knowing your child” is not the same as being able to:

  • Design and deliver a complete K–12 curriculum.
  • Identify and remedy cognitive or developmental issues.
  • Ensure exposure to knowledge beyond your own beliefs or expertise.

We do not allow parents to opt out of child safety seats, vaccinations (in most settings), or medical care for life-threatening conditions simply by declaring they know best. The state intervenes when the child’s welfare is at stake. Education is likewise fundamental to welfare and future autonomy. Ensuring professional, regulated schooling is part of that responsibility.

Parents still have enormous influence: they can help with homework, choose among schools (public vs. private, various pedagogical models), and inculcate family values at home. But they should not have unilateral power to completely control and limit their children’s education.

2. “Homeschooling is necessary for religious freedom.”

Religious freedom protects the right to practice one’s faith, not the right to withhold basic education from children or raise them in total isolation from other viewpoints. A ban on homeschooling need not:

  • Ban religious schools.
  • Ban religious instruction at home.
  • Ban children from practicing their faith.

What it does is ensure that every child, regardless of religion, learns core academic subjects and encounters some diversity of perspectives in a supervised environment. Parents can still:

  • Send children to religiously affiliated schools that meet state standards.
  • Teach their beliefs at home before and after school.
  • Participate in religious communities.

Religious freedom is not a license to deny children exposure to the broader world or to shield them from all information that might conflict with the parents’ doctrine.

3. “Some children are bullied or unsafe in schools; homeschooling protects them.”

Bullying, violence, and unsafe school environments are serious problems, but they require systemic solutions, not mass withdrawal. The right response is to:

  • Strengthen anti-bullying policies and enforcement.
  • Increase counseling, mental health services, and adult supervision.
  • Allow transfers to other schools or specialized programs when needed.
  • Improve training for staff on addressing harassment and inclusion.

A legal framework could allow narrowly tailored exceptions—such as temporary home-based instruction—under strict state oversight for children with documented medical or safety conditions, coupled with a plan to transition to a regulated institutional setting when feasible. But this is fundamentally different from an unregulated right to homeschool for any reason, indefinitely.

We do not dismantle traffic laws because some roads are dangerous; we improve the roads. Similarly, we fix schools; we do not privatize education child by child and hope it works out.

4. “Some homeschoolers achieve high academic results.”

There are certainly cases where homeschooling produces impressive academic outcomes, often in families with high education levels, ample resources, and strong motivation. But public policy must be designed for all children, not just the best-case scenarios.

A policy that relies on homeschooling effectively says:

  • If you have capable, educated, well-resourced parents, you might get an excellent education at home.
  • If you have abusive, neglectful, or ill-equipped parents, you might receive almost no education—and no one will stop it.

This variability is unacceptable when what’s at stake is a child’s entire future. Public policy should protect the worst-off children, not only enable the best-off to tailor their circumstances.

Those who want a distinctive educational approach can still choose:

  • Special-focus schools (arts, STEM, language immersion, etc.).
  • Private schools with different pedagogical philosophies.
  • Alternative public programs that maintain state standards and oversight.

The benefits a small number of families gain from unregulated homeschooling do not justify the systemic risks it poses to children’s rights and welfare.

VII. A Path Forward: Universal School Attendance with Strong Oversight

A legal ban on homeschooling should be accompanied by policies that respect pluralism, support families, and ensure high-quality options:

  1. Mandatory attendance in state-regulated schools (public or private) for all children, with:

    • Clear academic standards.
    • Periodic standardized assessments.
    • External accreditation and inspection.

  2. Pluralistic school options, including:

    • Public schools with varied programs.
    • Accredited private and religious schools.
    • Specialized schools for specific needs or interests.

  3. Targeted exceptions, strictly regulated, for:

    • Severe medical conditions requiring home-based instruction.
    • Temporary crises, with oversight and a plan for reintegration.

  4. Stronger child protection systems in schools:

    • Training for all school staff as mandated reporters.
    • Easy, confidential mechanisms for children to report abuse.
    • Coordination with social services and mental health support.

  5. Investment in quality:

    • Adequate funding to ensure safe, well-staffed, and inclusive schools everywhere.
    • Support for teachers’ professional development and fair compensation.

With such a framework, banning homeschooling does not mean forcing all children through a single rigid model. It means ensuring that every educational path is supervised, accountable, and designed to protect children’s rights and development.

Conclusion

Homeschooling, as a legally unregulated or lightly regulated option, places too much power in parents’ hands and too much risk on children’s shoulders. It allows enormous variability in educational quality, leaves many children invisible to mandatory reporters, facilitates abuse and extreme indoctrination, and undermines social cohesion and civic integration.

A complete legal ban on homeschooling, accompanied by robust and pluralistic state-regulated schooling, affirms that:

  • Education is a right of the child, not merely a prerogative of the parent.
  • Society has a duty to guarantee every child a safe, comprehensive, and balanced education.
  • Children deserve exposure to peers, to diverse ideas, and to adults outside their families.
  • Protection from abuse and neglect requires that all children be regularly seen and supported by trained professionals.

In a complex, interconnected democracy, children must not be raised in educational isolation. Mandatory, regulated schooling for all is not simply a policy preference; it is a moral obligation toward the most vulnerable members of society and an investment in a more just, informed, and cohesive future.

  • Academic rigor – There is no guarantee of basic proficiency in literacy, math, science, or civic knowledge.

We would never accept a justice system where some children get full legal protections and others get whatever their parents decide justice should look like. Why do we accept an education system where some children have robust, monitored schooling, and others vanish into private arrangements that the state barely sees?

A nationwide ban on homeschooling is not about controlling parents. It is about ensuring that every child—rich or poor, urban or rural, religious or secular—has the same baseline access to a supervised, standardized education.

Socialization Is Not a Luxury

Children are not only learning algebra and grammar. They are learning how to live with other human beings.

In schools, children:

  • Encounter peers from different backgrounds
  • Learn to work in teams and resolve conflict
  • Experience adults beyond their parents: mentors, counselors, coaches
  • Practice civic life—debating, compromising, cooperating

When children are educated entirely at home, these experiences can be drastically limited or highly curated. Parents may restrict exposure to any ideas, cultures, or people they dislike. That is not “protecting” children; it is narrowing their world and shrinking their future.

A modern democracy cannot be sustained by citizens who never learned to interact with difference, who never had to sit in a classroom with someone unlike themselves, who never encountered a teacher who challenged their home-grown assumptions.

Standardized, supervised education in state-regulated schools is not just an academic project; it is the core training ground of democratic citizenship.

Protection from Abuse and Neglect

We must confront an uncomfortable truth: The absence of oversight can create perfect conditions for abuse.

When children are:

  • Kept out of school
  • Rarely seen by mandated reporters
  • Educated entirely within the home, with no independent adult contact

The chance that abuse, neglect, or extreme indoctrination will go unnoticed rises sharply. There are documented cases where “homeschooling” served as a cover story for long-term abuse. These are not isolated freak occurrences; they are the predictable consequence of a system designed to look the other way.

In a school setting, a bruised arm, a sudden change in behavior, or signs of chronic neglect are noticed by teachers, nurses, and counselors. Patterns emerge because children are seen, day after day, by adults trained and obligated to act. That safety net simply does not exist when a child’s world is confined to the home.

A society that takes children’s rights seriously does not permit educational arrangements that systematically remove them from public sight.

Education Is a Public Good, Not a Private Hobby

Some argue that education is a private family matter. It is not.

Education shapes:

  • The workforce that drives our economy
  • The voters who determine our laws
  • The neighbors, colleagues, and leaders we all depend on
  • The shared knowledge base that makes communication and cooperation possible

When we allow education to fragment into entirely private, unregulated efforts, we weaken the shared foundation of knowledge and values on which our society rests. We end up with adults whose understanding of history, science, and civic life differs not because of honest disagreement, but because they were never exposed to common factual baselines in the first place.

Standardized, supervised schooling is how we ensure that, despite our differences, we inhabit at least the same basic reality.

Addressing the Counterarguments

Some will say: “But I can do better than the public system.”
Others will say: “My values conflict with what schools teach.”
Still others: “My child has needs the schools have failed to meet.”

These concerns are real—and they point to a necessary conclusion: we must improve our schools, not abandon them.

If public schools are underfunded, we must fund them.
If curricula are flawed, we must reform them.
If special needs go unmet, we must expand services.

We should:

  • Invest in smaller class sizes and better teacher training
  • Allow for specialized programs, magnet schools, and alternative pedagogies within the regulated system
  • Strengthen mechanisms for parental involvement in school governance
  • Create more flexible public options—project-based learning, community schools, and other models—within the framework of professional oversight and shared standards

But we cannot respond to shortcomings in our public system by saying, “Those with the time, money, and energy may leave; those without are stuck.” That deepens inequality and abandons the most vulnerable children to whatever remains.

A ban on homeschooling, paired with serious investment in our schools, is a declaration that we will fix our system for everyone, not carve out private escape hatches for the few.

The Moral Test of a Society

We are often judged by how we treat our most vulnerable. Children are the most voiceless citizens we have. They do not vote. They do not write policy. They do not choose where they live, what they are taught, or how their days are structured.

When we permit homeschooling with minimal oversight, we are effectively saying:
“We will trust every parent completely, and if some children fall through the cracks—if they emerge illiterate, isolated, or abused—that is a price we are willing to pay.”

That is morally unacceptable.

Our duty is not to maximize adult freedom at the cost of children’s basic rights. Our duty is to guarantee that every child, without exception, is seen, taught, protected, and prepared for life in a complex, pluralistic society.

A Call to Action

So what must we do?

  1. Enact a nationwide ban on homeschooling as a primary mode of K–12 education. Education must take place in state-regulated institutions: public schools, and where permitted, private schools that meet the same core standards and oversight requirements.

  2. Establish strong, uniform national standards for curriculum, teacher qualifications, and student assessment, while still allowing local flexibility in how those standards are met.

  3. Invest heavily in our schools—especially in underserved communities—so that every family has access to safe, well-resourced, high-quality education close to home.

  4. Create structured pathways for parental involvement in schools, ensuring that families are partners in education, not replaced by it.

  5. Monitor and enforce attendance and welfare so that no child is invisible to the systems meant to protect them.

This is not a small reform. It is a foundational shift in how we think about education and children’s rights.

But it is necessary.

Closing

We cannot keep telling ourselves that what happens behind closed doors is “none of our business” when the futures of children—and the future of our society—are at stake.

A child’s mind is not private property. It is a public trust.

Let us build a nation where every child walks through the doors of a school that is safe, supervised, and accountable; where no child is hidden; where no education is left to chance.

Let us choose, together, to guarantee standardized, supervised, state-regulated education for all—and consign the isolation and risk of homeschooling to the past.

Thank you.

While traditional schools must meet rigorous accreditation standards, employ certified teachers, and follow evidence-based curricula, homeschooling operates in a regulatory vacuum in most jurisdictions.

In diverse classroom settings, children learn to collaborate with peers from different backgrounds, navigate complex social hierarchies, resolve conflicts, and develop the interpersonal skills essential for success in modern workplaces and democratic society.

Homeschooled children, by contrast, exist in an artificial bubble, primarily interacting with family members and a narrow circle of parent-selected associates. This controlled environment fails to prepare them for the real world's diversity and challenges. They miss critical developmental experiences: working on group projects with difficult teammates, standing up to peer pressure, learning from teachers with different teaching styles, and building resilience through both success and failure in a supportive but independent setting.

The "socialization" offered through homeschool co-ops and extracurricular activities cannot replicate the organic, sustained peer interactions that occur during a full school day. The result? Perhaps the most urgent argument against homeschooling concerns child welfare. Schools serve as society's primary mechanism for identifying abuse, neglect, and educational deprivation. Teachers, counselors, and administrators are trained mandatory reporters who observe children daily, notice changes in behavior or appearance, and can intervene when necessary.

Homeschooling removes this crucial safety net. Behind closed doors, without regular oversight, children may suffer abuse, educational neglect, or extreme isolation with no opportunity for intervention. In many places, a parent with no education beyond the eighth grade can legally assume full responsibility for teaching advanced mathematics, chemistry, foreign languages, and history—subjects that take trained teachers years of higher education to master.

The predictable result is radical inconsistency. While some homeschooled students thrive, the data that homeschool advocacy organizations frequently cite is plagued by self-selection bias. Families that voluntarily submit test scores tend to be those whose children perform well; families whose children are falling behind have no obligation—and no incentive—to report results. The 2014 study by Bartholet at Harvard Law School and a comprehensive review by the Coalition for Responsible Home Education both demonstrate that when researchers attempt to gather data from the full population of homeschooled students rather than from self-selected volunteers, the rosy picture deteriorates significantly. Many homeschooled children arrive at adulthood with gaping holes in their education, lacking basic scientific literacy or the mathematical competence necessary for higher education.

A society that mandates automobile safety inspections, food-handling certifications, and building codes because it recognizes that individual choice can produce collective harm ought to apply the same principle to the education of its children. Education is infrastructure. It is not a lifestyle preference.

The Expertise Deficit

Teaching is a profession for a reason. Effective instruction requires more than knowledge of content; it requires understanding of learning differences, cognitive development stages, assessment strategies, and differentiated instruction techniques. A loving parent is not, by virtue of love, equipped to identify dyslexia, design an appropriate intervention plan for a child with ADHD, or teach calculus at a level that prepares a student for university-level STEM coursework.

Proponents of homeschooling often counter that parents know their children best. This is a sentimental claim that, while emotionally resonant, confuses familiarity with expertise. A parent may know their child's favorite food; that does not make the parent a nutritionist. The conflation of intimacy with competence is a dangerous fallacy when children's futures are at stake.

II. Socialization Is Not Optional—It Is Foundational

The Developmental Science

Decades of developmental psychology research, from Vygotsky's zone of proximal development to contemporary work on social-emotional learning, confirm that children need sustained, structured interaction with diverse peers to develop empathy, conflict resolution skills, cooperative problem-solving abilities, and the capacity for navigating social complexity. Schools provide this environment organically: children are required to work with others they did not choose, negotiate differences in opinion, encounter authority figures outside the family, and learn to function within institutional norms—skills that are indispensable in workplaces, civic organizations, and democratic society at large.

Homeschool advocates often point to co-ops, sports leagues, and community groups as substitutes. These are inadequate replacements for several reasons. First, participation in such activities is voluntary and curated by parents, meaning children are typically exposed only to peers from ideologically similar families. This is socialization within a bubble, not socialization in any meaningful developmental sense. Second, these activities are intermittent, while the socialization that schools provide is daily and immersive. Third, co-ops and extracurriculars lack the structural elements of a school environment—navigating hallway dynamics, resolving lunchroom disputes, collaborating on group projects with assigned partners—that build resilience and social adaptability.

The Civic Dimension

Public education has historically served as the great meeting ground of a pluralistic society. In a classroom, the child of an atheist sits beside the child of an evangelical. The child of immigrants works alongside the child whose family has lived in the community for generations. This exposure is not incidental—it is a cornerstone of democratic citizenship. When parents withdraw children from this shared space, they fracture the social fabric. They create citizens who have never been required to engage seriously with people who think, worship, or live differently from their own families.

The long-term consequence of widespread homeschooling is the balkanization of society into ideological silos. At a time when democratic institutions worldwide are strained by polarization and tribalism, removing children from the one institution designed to bridge divides is not just educationally irresponsible—it is civically dangerous.

III. Children Need External Eyes: The Child Protection Argument

Schools as Safety Nets

This is perhaps the most urgent and least discussed argument against homeschooling. Schools are the single most important node in the child protection infrastructure. Teachers are mandatory reporters trained to recognize signs of physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, and neglect. School nurses monitor health and hygiene. Counselors identify mental health crises. Coaches notice unexplained injuries. The daily presence of these professionals in a child's life creates a web of accountability that is impossible to replicate in a home setting.

When a child is homeschooled, that web is severed entirely. The child's only consistent adult contacts are the very people from whom they might need protection. This is not a theoretical concern. Exposed cases have revealed horrific patterns. The Turpin family in California, where thirteen children were held captive and tortured by parents who registered as homeschoolers, is only the most publicized example. The Coalition for Responsible Home Education maintains a database of cases involving severe abuse and neglect in homeschooling families, including cases resulting in the deaths of children whose isolation meant that no one outside the family could intervene.

The structural problem is this: homeschooling does not create abuse, but it creates the conditions in which abuse can persist undetected. It removes children from the sight of every mandated reporter. It eliminates the daily interactions that allow trained adults to notice a child who flinches at sudden movements, who is always hungry, who wears long sleeves in summer, or who begins to withdraw socially. For children in abusive households, school is not merely an educational institution—it is a lifeline. Permitting homeschooling is, in effect, permitting parents to cut that lifeline.

The Inadequacy of Current Oversight

Some argue that the solution is better regulation rather than a ban—home visits, annual assessments, mandatory check-ins. This approach has been tried and has consistently failed. Home-visit mandates are expensive to enforce and easy to evade. Annual assessments capture only a snapshot and can be prepared for in a way that obscures year-round neglect of education. Social workers are already overburdened. The practical reality is that no regulatory framework can replicate the daily, granular oversight that institutional schooling provides. Half-measures leave children exposed.

IV. The Indoctrination Problem

Education Versus Programming

A child is not an extension of a parent's identity. A child is a future citizen with independent rights, including the right to an education that equips them to think critically, evaluate evidence, and form their own beliefs. Homeschooling, in a troubling number of cases, is explicitly motivated by a desire to control the information a child receives—to prevent exposure to evolution, to shield children from learning about diverse family structures, to embed a singular religious or political ideology so deeply that the child never develops the intellectual tools to question it.

This is not education. It is indoctrination. And while parents in a free society are entitled to their beliefs, they are not entitled to use those beliefs to restrict their children's intellectual development. The philosopher Joel Feinberg articulated the concept of the child's "right to an open future"—the idea that children have a right not to have important life options foreclosed by decisions made on their behalf before they are old enough to choose for themselves. When a parent teaches a child that the earth is six thousand years old, that climate change is a hoax, or that women's highest purpose is domestic submission—and simultaneously ensures the child never encounters a contradicting viewpoint—that parent is not exercising a right. That parent is violating one.

Accredited schools, even those with religious affiliations, are subject to curricular standards that include exposure to scientific consensus, diverse historical perspectives, and critical thinking methodologies. Homeschools, in most states, are subject to none. The result is that homeschooling functions, for a significant subset of practitioners, as a legal mechanism for intellectual isolation.

V. Addressing the Counterarguments

"Parental Rights"

The most common objection to a homeschooling ban is that it violates parental rights. This argument deserves serious engagement, but ultimately it fails because it misidentifies the right-holder. Children are not property. The rights in question are the children's rights—to education, to protection, to an open future. When parental rights conflict with children's rights, the children's rights must prevail. We already accept this principle in other domains: parents cannot deny medical treatment to a critically ill child, cannot send a child to work in a factory, cannot refuse to feed or shelter a child. Mandating school attendance is simply the educational equivalent of these already-established protections.

The Supreme Court's 1972 decision in Wisconsin v. Yoder, which permitted Amish families to withdraw children from school after the eighth grade, is frequently cited by homeschool defenders. But Yoder was a narrow ruling based on the specific history and communal structure of the Amish, and it has been criticized by legal scholars for decades. Justice Douglas's partial dissent made the essential point: the case considered only the parents' wishes, not the children's. A child raised in deliberate educational isolation has been denied the tools to freely choose whether to remain in that community or to leave.

"Failing Public Schools"

Proponents of homeschooling frequently argue that public schools are failing and that parents are rescuing their children from substandard institutions. This argument, where valid, is an argument for investing in and improving public schools, not for abandoning them. The appropriate response to a leaking roof is to fix the roof, not to move into an unregulated tent. Allowing homeschooling as an escape valve actually reduces political pressure to improve public education, creating a perverse dynamic in which the most motivated and resourced parents exit the system, leaving behind children whose families lack the means to do the same.

"High-Performing Homeschoolers"

Yes, some homeschooled students excel. Some go to elite universities. Some win spelling bees and science fairs. These anecdotes, however, do not constitute a policy argument. Some children who work in factories grow up to be successful entrepreneurs; that does not justify child labor. Policy must be designed for the population, not for the outliers. The question is not whether homeschooling can work in the best cases, but whether permitting it as a legal category produces acceptable outcomes across the full range of cases. The evidence—incomplete precisely because of the lack of oversight—suggests it does not.

VI. International Precedent

A ban on homeschooling is not radical by international standards. Germany has effectively prohibited homeschooling since 1919, with the Weimar Republic recognizing that universal school attendance was essential for social cohesion and democratic citizenship. Sweden banned homeschooling in 2010 except in extraordinary circumstances. The Netherlands, Spain, and other European nations impose severe restrictions. These countries have not descended into tyranny; they have recognized that children's access to education is too important to be left to the unregulated discretion of individual households.

VII. Conclusion

The ban I am proposing is not born of hostility toward parents. Most parents who homeschool do so out of genuine concern for their children's well-being. But good intentions are insufficient grounds for public policy. The structural deficiencies of homeschooling—the absence of professional instruction, the loss of socialization in a diverse environment, the elimination of child-protection oversight, and the risk of ideological indoctrination—are not problems that can be fixed through regulation. They are inherent in the model itself.

Every child in this country deserves a qualified teacher, a classroom of diverse peers, and the protective gaze of mandated reporters who can intervene when something goes wrong. Every child deserves an education that opens the future rather than narrowing it. Every child deserves to be seen.

A society that truly values its children will stop treating their education as a matter of parental preference and start treating it as what it is: a non-negotiable public obligation. Homeschooling should be banned—not because parents cannot be trusted, but because children cannot be abandoned to the unaccountable discretion of any single authority, no matter how loving.

The stakes are too high, and the children are too important.
